implementation_notes: concurrent-ruby supplies both halves: Concurrent::Map is the thread-safe map and its compute_if_absent(key) block is the compute-if-absent step, while Concurrent::Promises.future(...) returns a future that many threads may wait on (wait/value block until completion; value! re-raises the stored error). The idiom is to put the future into the map from inside compute_if_absent - never the computation itself - and to delete the key when the future settles. Without the gem, core Ruby gives Mutex + ConditionVariable (and Thread::Queue) for the same structure, which is the hand-written form.
code_sketch:
INFLIGHT = Concurrent::Map.new

def load(key, &fetch)
  fut = INFLIGHT.compute_if_absent(key) do
    Concurrent::Promises.future(key, &fetch)      # leader starts the flight
  end
  fut.on_fulfill { |_| INFLIGHT.delete(key) }     # forget on success
  fut.on_reject  { |_| INFLIGHT.delete(key) }     # ... and on failure
  fut.value!                                      # shared value or raised error
end
pitfalls: The compute_if_absent block must only register the shared handle (a future), never run the slow work: the map's per-key synchronization must not be held for the duration of a remote call.
MRI's GVL makes Ruby threads cooperate, so coalescing removes duplicate I/O and duplicate work in other threads but does not give parallel computation; CPU-bound duplicates want a process pool.
Ractors (Ruby 3) cannot share the registry - each Ractor needs its own - so coalescing does not cross Ractor boundaries.
A rejected future whose value is never retrieved may surface only as an unhandled promise rejection; every waiter that calls value! gets the same exception instance.
The registry is per process: multi-worker servers (Puma, Unicorn, Sidekiq) do not deduplicate across workers, so a shared cache must absorb cross-process stampedes.
